newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. CEO's under gun to deliver quickly.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. CEO's under gun to deliver quickly.

text.p: It's not unusual for a struggling U.S. corporation to bring in a new leader from outside the company to turn the business around, but lately these hired guns are under increasing pressure to produce results quickly.

"If a company is in a turnaround situation, you don't give a new chief executive any more than a year to prove himself," said Quinn Spitzer, chief executive of Kepner Tregoe Inc, a Princeton, N.J.-based management consulting firm. "If they don't show their stuff real early they're going to be out."

Fueling the change has been the rise of institutional ownership of large chunks of U.S. corporations. Whether the institutions are pension funds or mutual funds, those in charge have a performance orientation. In an era of a soaring stock market, nobody has the patience to stay with a stodgy stock while managers hesitate to make meaningful changes in strategy.

Those getting the boot in recent weeks include Gilbert Amelio, ousted as chief executive of Apple Computer Inc, and John Walter, out as number two executive at AT&T and designated heir to AT&T chief executive Robert Allen.
Another chief executive recently shown the door was Ronald Allen of Delta Air Lines Inc. His situation differed from the others because he was a 34-year employee of the airline.
But now industry speculation is that Delta will turn to someone from outside of the company and maybe outside of the airline industry to find a permanent replacement.
The most unusual situation of all was that of John Walter who was brought into AT&T less than a year ago with the agreement that he would succeed Robert Allen in January, 1998.

The AT&T board, which itself has now come in for some sharp criticism, decided Walter was not the right man after less than one year on the job. Analysts now say that Allen's already bruised reputation has been further harmed by the embarrassing turn of events, and when the board finds another person for the top job, it will be time for Allen to move on.

George Fisher, who came to Eastman Kodak Co more than three years ago, has received high marks for his restructuring steps. But after a shortall in Kodak's second-quarter earnings July 16, the outlook for his tenure became a little murky.

Fisher said in a statement he was committed to staying with Kodak at least through the year 2000. Kodak said, in a separate statement that its statement was a response to speculation that Fisher might take the CEO job at AT&T.

One chief executive who boasts of having pulled aff a remarkable turnaround in just a year is Al Dunlap, who was brought in to revive the struggling appliance maker Sunbeam Corp. "We hit the ground running," he said in an interview July 23 as the company announced that earnings per share from continuing operations in the second quarter soared to $0.30 per share from $0.03 a year ago on a 16.6 percent sales increase.

Dunlap said he installed a team of new managers who reduced the number of factories, reconfigured the computer system, sold or closed non-strategic businesses and opened new international distribution channels.
Dunlap, who has presided over turnarounds at Scott Paper and other companies, said the chief executive must be backed by a board of directors that legitimately wants to make the change.
Dunlap said part of the problems that have plagued companies like Eastman Kodak, AT&T and Apple Computer can be attributed to boardroom inertia.
Experts say the trend to stock ownership concentrated in the hands of big institutional investors has been accompanied by a focus on the board of directors as the ultimate decision-maker.
But what happens if the chief executive and the board disagree?

"The board's job is to hire, monitor, compensate and fire the chief executive," said Ira Millstein, a partner at the New York law firm Weil Gotshal & Manges who has been speaking out on corporate governance issues for years.
One chief executive who says he is comfortable with an active, no-nonsense board is Marshall Carter, who is chairman of Boston's State Street Corp.

Although his predecessor at State Street, William Edgerly, made the initial approach in 1991 to woo him from Chase Manhattan Bank, the board of directors was very much involved in the recruitment process. "He (Edgerly) said 'can you come to Boston this weekend to meet members of the board?'," Carter recalled in a recent interview. "The very second meeting, and four subsequent meetings, were always with the board or half of the board. They really grilled me."

The State Street board has the power to oversee succession of the chief executive, and even promotions at the vice president, senior vice president and executive vice president level. Carter said he is happy with the arrangement and observes that in the case of a 205-year-old company like State Street, "indivduals are just a little pinprick in the time sequence."
Millstein said that a board by its very nature is one step removed from management and has an opportunity to see weaknesses in management that managers themselves may not be able to see.
He said while the boards of directors are much more professional today than before, "there are plenty who have not gotten there yet. I can't tell you we've reached the millennium."

More than any other issue, the biggest battles in corporate America have been over succession. Cyrus Freidheim, a partner at the management consulting firm Booz Allen & Hamilton, said "clearly the board has the responsibility" to pick a new chief executive. Even when a professional search firm is hired to find a new chief executive, he said, "the board should do all of the due diligence required to make sure it is the right choice."
The search by companies such as Apple Computer, AT&T and Delta Air Lines Inc for new leadership comes at a time when the role of the chief executive has been transformed.

"The chief executive today has to worry not about one company but alliances with companies scattered around the world," said Freidheim. He is required to be a statesman and a diplomat in addition to being a tough performance-driven manager of his own company." He believes any board deciding on a new leader based on the narrower performance criteria of the recent past "is making a terrible mistake".
